questions.stem: A bakery makes loaf P using $3$ kg of flour and loaf Q using $2$ kg of flour. At most $90$ kg of flour is available per day, and $x$ loaves of P and $y$ loaves of Q are baked. The flour restriction is
questions.explanation: Flour used is $3$ kg per loaf of P times $x$ plus $2$ kg per loaf of Q times $y$, giving $3x + 2y$ kg. Since no more than $90$ kg is available, this total must be at most $90$: $3x + 2y \le 90$.

optionRationale.2: The coefficients are swapped; P uses $3$ kg and Q uses $2$ kg.
optionRationale.3: A resource limit is an upper bound, so the inequality sign must be $\le$.
optionRationale.4: This counts loaves instead of kilograms of flour, ignoring the different usage per loaf.

questions.objective: Translate a resource limit into a linear inequality

questions.stem: A canteen buys $x$ kg of food F1 at ₹8 per kg and $y$ kg of food F2 at ₹12 per kg and must buy at least $40$ kg in all. If the canteen wants the lowest cost, the objective function is
questions.explanation: The total cost is the sum of price times quantity, $8x + 12y$ rupees, and the canteen wants the lowest cost, so $Z = 8x + 12y$ is minimised. The condition $x + y \ge 40$ is a constraint, not the objective.

optionRationale.2: The prices are attached to the wrong foods; F1 costs ₹8, not ₹12.
optionRationale.3: The aim is the lowest cost, so the function is minimised, not maximised.
optionRationale.4: $x + y$ is the total quantity, which is limited by a constraint, not the cost.

questions.objective: Write the objective function of a diet problem

questions.stem: A workshop makes lamp A (profit ₹50) and lamp B (profit ₹40). Lamp A needs $2$ hours of cutting and $4$ hours of assembly; lamp B needs $3$ hours of cutting and $1$ hour of assembly. Cutting time is at most $120$ hours and assembly time at most $100$ hours. The maximum profit is
questions.explanation: With $x$ lamps A and $y$ lamps B: $2x + 3y \le 120$ and $4x + y \le 100$. The corners are $(0,0)$, $(25,0)$, $(18,28)$ and $(0,40)$ with profits $0$, $1250$, $2020$ and $1600$. The maximum ₹2,020 occurs at $x = 18$, $y = 28$.

optionRationale.2: ₹1,600 is the profit when only lamp B is made, at the corner $(0,40)$.
optionRationale.3: ₹1,250 is the profit when only lamp A is made, at the corner $(25,0)$.
optionRationale.4: ₹2,150 exceeds every corner value and is not attainable within the limits.

questions.stem: A diet needs at least $10$ units of vitamin V1 and at least $15$ units of vitamin V2. A unit of food P gives $1$ of V1 and $3$ of V2 and costs ₹4; a unit of food Q gives $2$ of V1 and $1$ of V2 and costs ₹3. The least cost of the diet is
questions.explanation: With $x$ units of P and $y$ of Q: $x + 2y \ge 10$ and $3x + y \ge 15$. The corner points of this unbounded region are $(0,15)$, $(4,3)$ and $(10,0)$, with costs $45$, $25$ and $40$. The least is ₹25 at $(4,3)$.

optionRationale.1: ₹20 corresponds to $(5,0)$, which fails the vitamin V1 requirement.
optionRationale.2: ₹40 is the cost at the corner $(10,0)$, not the least cost.
optionRationale.3: ₹45 is the cost at $(0,15)$, the most expensive corner.

questions.objective: Solve a diet problem for minimum cost

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In a diet problem with only $\ge$ type nutrient constraints, the minimum cost exists even though the feasible region is unbounded.
Reason (R): Both the cost coefficients and the nutrient requirements are non-negative, so the cost cannot decrease without limit.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The region defined by $\ge$ constraints stretches to infinity, but the cost $Z = ax + by$ with $a, b > 0$ only grows as $x$ or $y$ grow. Thus $Z$ is bounded below by $0$ and attains its least value at a corner point, and the reason is exactly why the minimum exists.

optionRationale.2: The reason is not just true; boundedness of $Z$ from below is what guarantees the minimum.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true: positive costs prevent $Z$ from decreasing indefinitely.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true: the minimum is attained at a corner of the region.

questions.objective: Justify the existence of a minimum over an unbounded region

questions.stem: Match the type of linear programming problem in List-I with the typical form of its constraints in List-II.

right: I. Limits on the total money and a minimum amount in the safer scheme
II. Minimum requirement of each nutrient, expressed with $\ge$
III. Supply from each godown must not be exceeded and each shop's demand must be met
IV. Limited machine and labour hours, expressed with $\le$

questions.explanation: A manufacturing problem is limited by scarce resources such as machine or labour hours ($\le$), which is IV. A diet problem needs minimum nutrients ($\ge$), which is II. A transportation problem must respect supply and meet demand (III). An investment problem has a budget cap with a minimum in the safer option (I).

optionRationale.1: Items A and B have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.
optionRationale.3: Items C and D have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.
optionRationale.4: Items A and C have been interchanged; check each pairing against its definition.

questions.objective: Link LPP types with their constraint structure

questions.stem: A person invests up to ₹1,20,000 in bonds (return $7\%$) and shares (return $11\%$). At least ₹36,000 must go into bonds and at most ₹80,000 into shares. The maximum yearly return is
questions.explanation: Let bonds be $x$ and shares $y$: $x + y \le 120000$, $x \ge 36000$, $y \le 80000$. The best corner is $(40000, 80000)$, giving $0.07 \times 40000 + 0.11 \times 80000 = 2800 + 8800 = ₹11{,}600$. The share cap prevents putting everything into the higher-return option.

optionRationale.1: ₹11,320 is the return at $(36000, 80000)$, which leaves ₹4,000 uninvested.
optionRationale.2: ₹8,400 is the return if the whole amount goes into bonds only.
optionRationale.4: ₹13,200 would need the entire ₹1,20,000 in shares, which breaks the ₹80,000 cap.

questions.stem: A unit of item X yields profit ₹30 and a unit of item Y yields ₹25. The restrictions are $2x + y \le 100$ (material), $x + 2y \le 80$ (labour) and $x + y \le 45$ (storage), with $x, y \ge 0$. The maximum profit is
questions.explanation: The corner points are $(0,0)$, $(45,0)$, $(10,35)$ and $(0,40)$, with profits $0$, $1350$, $1175$ and $1000$. The maximum ₹1,350 is at $(45,0)$. The storage line cuts off the meeting point $(40,20)$ of the other two lines, which would otherwise give ₹1,700.

optionRationale.1: ₹1,175 is the profit at $(10,35)$, where storage and labour meet.
optionRationale.2: ₹1,000 is the profit when only item Y is made, at $(0,40)$.
optionRationale.3: ₹1,700 comes from $(40,20)$, which violates the storage restriction $x + y \le 45$.

questions.stem: A feed mix must satisfy $2x + y \ge 14$, $x + 3y \ge 15$ and $x + y \ge 8$ (all in suitable units) with $x, y \ge 0$, where $x$ and $y$ are quantities of two ingredients costing ₹7 and ₹6 per unit. The minimum cost is
questions.explanation: The first two lines meet at $(27/5, 16/5)$, which also satisfies $x + y = 43/5 \ge 8$, so the third constraint is redundant. The corners $(0,14)$, $(27/5, 16/5)$ and $(15,0)$ have costs $84$, $57$ and $105$. The minimum is $7(27/5) + 6(16/5) = ₹57$.

optionRationale.1: ₹84 is the cost at the corner $(0,14)$, which is not the cheapest.
optionRationale.2: ₹105 is the cost at $(15,0)$, the dearest corner.
optionRationale.4: ₹60 is the cost of the whole-unit mix $(6,3)$, which is feasible but not the cheapest.

questions.objective: Find a fractional corner solution of a diet LPP

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about linear programming problems.
A. In a transportation problem the total transport cost is a linear function of the quantities shipped.
B. The feasible region of a diet problem is always bounded.
C. For a maximisation problem with only $\le$ constraints and positive right-hand sides, the origin is a feasible point.
D. If an optimal solution exists, it can be found only at an interior point of the feasible region.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: A is true: cost is the sum of unit cost times quantity. C is true since $0 \le b$ holds for every positive right-hand side. B is false because $\ge$ constraints leave the region open-ended, and D is false because the optimum is always sought at a corner point, not an interior point.

optionRationale.1: B is false: a diet region built from $\ge$ constraints is unbounded.
optionRationale.3: B is false, so this pair cannot be correct, and C is true but missing from A and B.
optionRationale.4: D is false: an optimal solution lies at a corner point, not at an interior point.

questions.stem: Godown G1 holds $40$ units and G2 holds $30$ units; shop S1 needs $25$ units and S2 needs $35$ units. Cost per unit (₹): G1 to S1 is $6$, G1 to S2 is $4$, G2 to S1 is $3$, G2 to S2 is $5$. If $x$ and $y$ units go from G1 to S1 and S2 respectively, the minimum total transportation cost is
questions.explanation: Shipments are $x, y$ from G1 and $25 - x$, $35 - y$ from G2, so the cost is $6x + 4y + 3(25 - x) + 5(35 - y) = 250 + 3x - y$ with $30 \le x + y \le 40$, $0 \le x \le 25$, $0 \le y \le 35$. The least value is at $(0, 35)$: $250 - 35 = ₹215$.

optionRationale.2: ₹220 is the cost at $(0,30)$, which sends $5$ fewer units on the cheap G1-S2 route.
optionRationale.3: ₹230 is the cost at $(5,35)$, which wastes units on the dear G1-S1 route.
optionRationale.4: ₹250 is the cost when $x = y = 0$, which breaks the demand requirement $x + y \ge 30$.
